speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Clearly the demand is strong. We recognize that, but our focus is on making sure that we can orderly increase our production ramp up, bring our supply chain along so that we can deliver on our commitments, and deliver on our commitments with excellent profitability. That's our first priority.
finding: Already in 2006, with 2007 slots 98% sold, Boeing put orderly, profitable ramp-ups with the supply chain ahead of chasing demand.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Clearly we have about 18 million or 19 million shares to go under our current authorization. The plan will be to go back to the Board and ask for an additional authorization. We will buy accordingly, as long as the stock is undervalued as it is, we will continue to have a pretty active buyback program.
finding: Boeing's buyback rule was value-based (buy while the stock looks undervalued), and it kept buybacks steady through the 2006-08 period.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Well, clearly it's a competitive environment, but we're really pleased with the kinds of deals we're signing. We believe we have embedded in those deals a real opportunity to create real value going forward, Steve, so we're not having fire sales.
finding: By 2006 Boeing said it had moved from aggressive discounting to value pricing on its order-boom deals.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: we're clearly not there yet. We will continually be working with our customers, because that's where a product development decision is going to start and end ... Right now, Steve, we're just enjoying the success of the 737. ... We've got over 6,000 of them on order.
finding: In 2006 Boeing had not decided on a 737 replacement (single- or twin-aisle), would let customers drive that decision, and was content to keep selling the current 737.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: we do have a good agreement with them and a good arrangement that we're working with them to really provide us access to titanium, but they’re not our only titanium supplier. We do have others that we have agreements with that will help us to offset that risk.
finding: Boeing multi-sourced critical raw materials such as titanium (VSMPO plus others) to hedge supply-bottleneck risk.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: our performance score is based on how well we deliver economic profit for the corporation, and one of the levers there are assets, and working capital as well. So we have a lot of focus across the corporation, because that's not only the score for our executives, it's also the score for our salaried employees
finding: Boeing tied executive and salaried pay to economic profit, including asset and working-capital efficiency, which gave everyone an incentive for capital-efficient decisions.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We are well downstream on this development program. We're well within the budget, well within the business case, and it really does look good. Stanley, all I can tell you is that right now, this looks like the best-run development program I've ever seen
finding: In April 2006 Boeing called the 787 its best-run development program and within budget; the later overruns and delays reversed this view.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We have a global supply chain that has to be taken into consideration. They're not sitting around just waiting for us to up production. They do have other work and other requirements. ... It's not something that you can turn on immediately.
finding: Boeing saw rate increases as long-lead decisions constrained by shared suppliers' other commitments, so capacity cannot be added quickly.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: The 767, I think we still have a few orders yet to produce. I don't know the exact date, but some time towards the end of the year we'll be taking a look at it.
finding: In April 2006 Boeing had only a few 767 orders left to build and planned to review the line's future by year-end; the 767 was near a shutdown decision.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think the revamped 350 concept that we are seeing I do not think fundamentally changes what we are doing. We have two pretty good-sized book-ends on either side of their airplane.
finding: Boeing's first reaction to the relaunched A350 was to hold its product plan unchanged, relying on 787 and 777 bracketing it.
trigger: Airbus relaunched A350 concept (Farnborough, July 2006)
response: No change to Boeing product strategy; rely on 787 and 777 as book-ends

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We expected competition in our business plans, obviously, and I think the revamped 350 concept that we are seeing I do not think fundamentally changes what we are doing. We have two pretty good-sized book-ends on either side of their airplane.
finding: Boeing's immediate response to the A350 XWB launch was no change in strategy, relying on the 787 and 777 on either side of it.
trigger: A350 XWB launch at Farnborough (July 2006)
response: No change to product strategy; rely on 787/777 book-ends

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have to balance orders with supply chain, with development considerations, and yes, there is upward pressure on our current production plans. ... the unprecedented demand for this airplane is forcing us to ask the question. ... over the next year or so, we will come up with a final answer there.
finding: Boeing considered extra 787 capacity (possibly a second line) but made the decision subject to the supply chain and development, over about a year.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: on the so-called Dash-10 787 growth, we have a number of customers who are discussing with us -- some would say pushing us -- to develop that plane. I think when the timing is right, in all likelihood, we will.
finding: Asked how to counter the A350 at the top of the 787 and bottom of the 777, Boeing pointed to a likely 787-10 stretch driven by customers.
trigger: A350 XWB targeting large-787/small-777 segment
response: Plan 787-10 stretch derivative when timing is right

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: By the way, this is not a big engineering bill, to take our core 787 and extend it to a Dash-10. It is real money but it does not compare with the base models. ... it is more of a derivative type of economics.
finding: Boeing preferred cheap derivative stretches (787-10) to answer rivals rather than new clean-sheet spending.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: They have skin in this game to, so the extent to which we [achieve] together, that they are falling behind in some area or where the weight is an issue in another, yes, it is their resources that they are applying. That is part of our agreement with them.
finding: Under the 787 risk-sharing contracts, suppliers were expected to fund their own recovery work, which pushed development risk onto partners.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The facts are that our business model is not being met. ... we are asking a series of fundamental questions now on a going-forward basis -- restructure, terminate, affiliate being the obvious options, but continuing to operate as we are now is not an option.
finding: McNerney's rule for a venture missing its business model (Connexion) was to restructure, terminate or partner, and never to carry on unchanged.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: As I pointed out, Dominic, we are just seeking a level playing field here, equally applied regulatory environment for both. ... I think our customer and the legislature behind it are probably the ones that should push for this rather than us.
finding: In the tanker contest Boeing pressed regulatory asymmetries (ITAR, anti-bribery rules) against EADS but left the public push to Congress and the customer.
trigger: Northrop/EADS rival tanker bid
response: Advocate level regulatory playing field via legislature/customer

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We are studying where to go and obviously composites are one of the technologies that could flow from the 787 down into the narrow body. ... whatever plane we define for the future aero body -- which will not be for a number of years, keep in mind
finding: In 2006 Boeing framed a 737 replacement as years away and built on 787 composite technology.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I'd say the 50% looks pretty good, and there is upward pressure in our planning on production rates. Exactly where that sorts out will be a function of what the other guys do
finding: Boeing kept a 50% share assumption for the 787 niche and said its production-rate increases would depend on what Airbus did.
trigger: A350 XWB not delivering until 2014-15, leaving 787 alone in mid-size niche
response: Upward pressure on 787 production rates, calibrated to Airbus moves

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: The 787 program continues to experience pressure with respect to weights and supplier implementation. We are raising our R&D forecast to reflect these increasing pressures as well as modified and increased scope on the 747-A program
finding: Weight and supplier-implementation problems on the 787 were visible by October 2006, a year before the first delay, and Boeing answered with more R&D money rather than a schedule change.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: we announced that we would discontinue our Connexion service by year end and take charges totaling approximately $320 million in the second half of 2006. ... This decision will add about $0.15 per share to EPS beginning in 2007
finding: Under McNerney, Boeing was willing to shut down an unprofitable venture (Connexion) and take a one-time charge to lift future EPS.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Major uses of our cash in the quarter included approximately $2.2 billion to complete the Aviall acquisition
finding: Boeing spent heavily on acquisitions to grow its aftermarket services business.

speaker: analyst (Morgan Stanley); Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the A350 XWB isn't going to deliver until the 2014 or 2015 timeframe, which gives you sole positioning in the mid-size wide-body niche ... I'd say the 50% looks pretty good, and there is upward pressure in our planning on production rates. Exactly where that sorts out will be a function of what the other guys do
finding: With the redesigned A350 XWB years away, Boeing kept a roughly 50% share assumption for the 787 niche and tied its 787 rate increases to Airbus's moves.
trigger: Airbus relaunched A350 as XWB with delivery ~2014-15
response: Upward pressure on 787 production-rate planning; hold ~50% share assumption

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: this program's projected economics are significantly better than any airplane program I have been involved with and that's because of the structure of the supply chain, both in its participation and recurring and nonrecurring costs.
finding: Before the delays, Boeing believed the 787 risk-sharing model, with partners carrying recurring and non-recurring costs, gave it unmatched program economics.

speaker: analyst (Credit Suisse); Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: you may have more opportunity here lately to capture some share just based on some instability perhaps in the marketplace right now, vis-à-vis a competitor. ... this is a derivative program, and the amount of money we're spending on this reflects that. I mean this is taking an airplane we know how to make
finding: Asked about gaining share from a rival's instability, Boeing stressed the 747-8 was a derivative with investment scaled to match, a low-cost way to compete at the top end.
trigger: Instability at Airbus (A380 problems) in 2006
response: Pursue 747-8 as a derivative, modest-investment program

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have a crystal clear view yet of what the narrow body market of the future is going to look like. ... there is a lot of discussion around the 100 packs ... a bigger version of a narrow body, you know, the 200-plus size as well as the core of the market, the 150 to 180.
finding: In 2006 Boeing had not settled the size of its next narrowbody (100, 150-180 or 200+ seats) and only matured technologies while internal camps debated.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have a 1,300 plane backlog with our current narrow body that we keep improving and spiraling technology into that makes the bar tougher for the newer airplane. ... it'll be an ongoing discussion that will be measured in years not months
finding: Boeing's large 737 backlog and continual upgrades raised the bar for a new narrowbody, so the replacement decision was years away.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: There will be some work that is going to be brought to Seattle. That was going to be done by a couple of our suppliers that is more efficiently done in Seattle, and so we've made an adjustment there, and that's the one we have triggered.
finding: Boeing's first funded 787 contingency (2006) was to insource systems-installation work from struggling suppliers back to Seattle.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In terms of the triple, I think we need to see what the A350 is or isn't before we can make a judgment on whether a competitive response is needed.
finding: Boeing chose wait-and-see on a 777 response until the A350 design was defined.
trigger: A350 XWB threat to the 777
response: Defer 777 response until A350 is defined

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if the A350 presents a legitimate competitive threat to certain parts of the 777 line, we would respond, and in all likelihood it would be some kind of a modification
finding: Boeing signalled its answer to the A350 would be a 777 modification, not a clean-sheet replacement.
trigger: A350 threat to parts of the 777 line
response: Likely 777 modification if threat proves real

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We now have 544 firm orders from 44 customers, which is the highest tally ever achieved by a commercial jet program within three years of its launch. ... We will remain on-track for first delivery to ANA in May of 2008.
finding: In April 2007 Boeing was still committing to the original May 2008 787 first delivery on record orders; this is the baseline for the delays that followed.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the two big areas that we will have to address at timing that is consistent with what customers need and the maturation of our technology ... are at some point narrow-body replacement ... the 777 will have to be modified somewhere along the line. Which comes first? I think what we are doing is maturing the technologies
finding: In 2007 Boeing saw two future moves, a narrowbody replacement and a 777 modification, and timed both to customer need and technology maturity rather than committing to either.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: two or three years ago we really were faced with a much more competitive pricing environment and also a phase we are trying to have pricing that bridge us to new market particularly for the 747-8 and then also we saw a more robust market in this time period for the 777
finding: During the earlier price war Boeing deliberately cut prices on the 747 and 777 to bridge to new programs and markets, trading margin for position.
trigger: Highly competitive pricing environment ~2004-05
response: Aggressive bridge pricing on 747/777 and single-aisle

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the narrow-body would be a major program, it's hard to predict exactly what we will or won't be doing to the 777. So, I think that the key point is that we will have created economic room to respond properly to those competitive environments through the productivity initiatives
finding: Boeing planned to fund a future narrowbody program and a 777 response from productivity-driven margin headroom, not new capital.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We have been encouraged to raise rates. But I have a fundamental belief, which is that the best customer service is to deliver on your promises. And so to raise rates and then later not be able to deliver because the supply chain was not with you ... is a lesson that this industry teaches itself every decade or so
finding: McNerney refused to raise rates faster despite customer pressure, putting supply-chain readiness and reliable delivery ahead of capturing demand.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The 78 is now end of 13-14 is where we are in terms of quoting any kind of a sizable quarter. In general, there is some exceptions to that, but it's about there. 737, I think we are out to about 11
finding: In early 2007 Boeing's skyline was sold out to 2013-14 on the 787 and to about 2011 on the 737.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we will see somebody probably in the narrow-body segment from China competing there. ... I am one of these people who believes that partnering with people who are potentially competitors is not necessarily a bad thing. So I think we will have a headset of both competing with them and partnering locally
finding: Boeing expected a Chinese narrowbody entrant within 10-20 years and was open to partnering with potential competitors.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: 787, anywhere from a 20% to 40% improvement in key metrics on the environmental footprint. We would have similar objectives for the next narrow-body and similar objectives for that day when we get around to the success for the 777.
finding: Boeing set a 787-like 20-40% improvement bar for a next narrowbody and a 777 successor, which implies it would wait for step-change technology rather than make incremental moves.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the aggressive pricing you are seeing today on the date of delivery. This year’s delivery that we entered into two or three years ago to bridge to a better market
finding: Boeing itself priced 777 deals aggressively in 2004-05 to bridge a weak market, and the cost showed up in deliveries years later.
trigger: Weak market and competitive campaigns two to three years earlier
response: Priced 777 aggressively to win orders; deferred production cost rose

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are raising R&D guidance for 2007 primarily to preserve the 787 schedule. This is absolutely the right thing to do because keeping our commitments to customers is paramount here.
finding: In mid-2007 Boeing chose to spend more R&D to protect the 787 schedule and treated customer commitments as worth the cost.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I am confident we are beyond what I will call the invention activities. We have proven the airplane's technologies, especially its large composite sections and its major systems. It took longer and cost more than planned
finding: Three months before the first 787 delay was announced, Boeing declared the invention phase over, which shows how overconfident its schedule view was.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: it’s always a tussle between waiting until you have the supply chain in the shape you want it to be before you go up on one hand and customer demand on the other. We’ll continue to be prudent but our bias is toward raising over time
finding: Boeing's rate rule weighed supply-chain readiness against demand: it wanted the supply chain in shape before raising rates, but its bias was upward over time (737, 787, 777).

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the current thinking is that there will be some technology insertions we can make that will effectively respond to an airplane that is already a little bit bigger than the A-350, the 1000. ... we have some technologies that we’ve based the 787 on and some other technologies that can be inserted in plenty of time
finding: Boeing's first answer to the A350-1000 was an incremental 777 upgrade using 787 technology, not a new airplane.
trigger: Airbus A350-1000 gained traction after the 2007 Paris Air Show, targeting long-range 777
response: Plan 777 technology insertions (derivative) rather than a new design
lag: 7-9 years before rival EIS; no urgency

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the rate increases that we have pursued this year have all gone smoothly. Raw material prices has stabilized, albeit at higher levels ... some of our major structural suppliers who are still looking for fasteners and bearings and hydraulic fittings and the like.
finding: Boeing's 2007 rate increases went smoothly, but lower-tier shortages (fasteners, bearings, fittings) remained a limit that Boeing managed directly.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: it is probably impacted somewhat by the A350, as customers are trying to assess precisely what that airplane’s performance can be for them. ... it would not surprise me if over the short- to medium-term, if we didn’t harden up into something that we began to offer people.
finding: Boeing held off launching the 787-10 while customers assessed the A350, offering a derivative only once customer requirements firmed up.
trigger: Airbus A350 performance claims affecting customer decisions
response: Delay 787-10 configuration and launch until requirements firm

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: as long as we think our stock is a good value, which we still think it is, we will consider it up in the temple ... our primary strategy is organic growth ... I don’t think it is all that bad to just grow a little cash balance either. In case something does go really, really bad
finding: Boeing's capital allocation order was organic investment, then buybacks when the stock looked cheap, then bolt-on M&A, while keeping a cash cushion for shocks.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: if you are asking is there something there for 777 in response YEN to an A-350, probably not distinctly. I think there is something that we would have to deal with generic kinds of things that could be devoted to that for some initial studies if needed
finding: Boeing's 2008 R&D plan held no dedicated money for a 777 response to the A350, only generic funds for initial studies.
trigger: Airbus A350 XWB
response: Only initial study money; no funded 777 program

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the new plan reinserts normal margins in the schedule for dealing with issues we might uncover in our remaining ground or flight testing. In support of our new plan, we are placing additional Boeing people at our supplier facilities
finding: The original 787 schedule had stripped out normal schedule margin; the October 2007 re-plan put it back and sent Boeing staff into suppliers.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In making the decision to bring in Pat Shanahan to take over the leadership for the 787 ... We also recognized that we're at a stage where a different set of strengths is needed to bring it all home.
finding: Boeing's first response to the 787 slip was to replace program leadership with an execution-focused manager.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We also stepped up the pace of share repurchase during the quarter by investing $905 million to buyback over 9 million shares. For the first nine months we have repurchased 19.6 million shares for $1.9 billion.
finding: Boeing accelerated buybacks in the same quarter it announced the first 787 delay.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Total Boeing revenue guides for 2008 is reduced to between $67.5 billion and $68.5 billion due to the moving approximately 35 Dreamliner deliveries from 2008 into 2009.
finding: The first 787 re-plan (October 2007) moved about 35 deliveries into 2009; by April 2008 the shift had grown to about 75, showing the slips escalating.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: increasing our 2008 forecast to between $3.2 billion and $3.4 billion from between $2.8 and $3 billion. Approximately half of the increase is due to the 787 schedule change
finding: 2008 R&D guidance rose repeatedly, from $2.8-3.0B to $3.2-3.4B (October 2007) to $3.6-3.8B (April 2008), as 787 and 747-8 problems grew.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: obviously we want the supply chain focused on helping us get these first airplanes through and built and so we're not pressing as hard as we might otherwise be at the different stage in the program.
finding: During the 787 crisis Boeing held back on settling supplier claims so partners could stay focused on delivering the first airplanes.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We can get back to you with a better number, but its somewhere in the 55 to 65 range.
finding: Boeing kept the 787 supply chain producing through the delay and expected to build 55-65 aircraft before first delivery, a large inventory and rework exposure.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We still think the initial units will be profitable. ... we do know and still feel that those initial units will be profitable, but they will be diluted from a margin standpoint to our marked mature material programs.
finding: In October 2007 Boeing said early 787s would be profitable; by April 2008 it had cut that to a zero booking margin, a reversal after further delays.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think there is a low probability that we would change the timing of that discussion ... I think we are in a rhythm of working together with the union to come up with the successful negotiation and that's what I anticipate quite frankly.
finding: Boeing chose not to pull forward the September 2008 IAM negotiation despite the critical 787 timing and relied on its working rhythm with the union.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we were surprised on the physical reality of some of the things that we received from suppliers versus the documentation we realized, we really needed to work with them to make sure we had better visibility on the build
finding: The 787 partner model failed partly because Boeing relied on supplier paperwork instead of physically verifying work, which it then fixed by deploying manufacturing and procurement staff.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: a claim [ph] totaled by the end of '09, our current target is 109, versus 112 which was the original schedule so, three being pushed into 10 net impact.
finding: In October 2007 Boeing still targeted 109 cumulative 787 deliveries by end-2009 (against 112 originally); by April 2008 it expected only about 25 in 2009, showing how optimistic early re-plans were.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: as some pressure on the engineering population occurred due to the 87 push out, I think we had to tap into other parts of Boeing and that's one of the advantages of our size. Other parts of Boeing to staff some of the -8 work
finding: Boeing handled engineering shortages by moving engineers between units (including defense), treating its size as a buffer against talent constraints.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think there had been some analyst projections that said that 08 would be the crossover year but quite frankly, I do not think we ever characterize it one way or the other.
finding: Boeing declined to set a public target for overtaking Airbus in deliveries.
trigger: Analyst expectation that 2008 would be the delivery crossover year vs Airbus
response: Refused to commit to a delivery-leadership target

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: increasing our dividend 14% and authorizing a new $7 billion share repurchase program. We see more potential to return capital through share repurchase and dividends as our financial performance gets even stronger.
finding: At the 2007 peak Boeing committed to large buybacks and dividend growth while the 787 was still in development.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: with high fuel prices and aging fleets, the US carriers who have not yet responded during this replacement cycle have an acute need to do so, and we expect them to order airplanes over the next couple of years.
finding: Boeing's demand thesis relied on high fuel prices and aging US fleets driving a replacement wave.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: BCA delivered 112 airplanes in the fourth quarter and 441 for the year. ... Operating margins expanded to 10.7%. BCA’s backlog grew 46% to more than $255 billion on record orders
finding: In 2007 Boeing combined record orders with double-digit commercial margins.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Our plans are more than fully funded at 110% of our projected benefit obligation. We have reduced risk profile on our pension plans by transitioning our asset allocation to less volatile asset classes.
finding: Boeing de-risked its pension assets before the 2008 crash, which later limited the damage.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Boeing’s debt levels continue to decline during the year as maturing debt was not refinanced due to our strong cash position. ... Financial strength and solid credit ratings are priorities for us and we continue to enjoy the highest ratings in the industry.
finding: Boeing paid down debt instead of refinancing and treated top credit ratings as a priority, a conservative balance-sheet stance.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: we are always looking at better ways to provide value to our share holders with that cash and that can include some things like you have seen in the past, particularly with the addition of AVO ... how we could look at our strategy in terms of being horizontally versus vertically integrated.
finding: With about $12B of cash, Boeing weighed buybacks against acquisitions and against rethinking its degree of vertical integration.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the model that will compete for the long-range 777’s if the plane has the performance that AirBus thinks it can have is the 1000 and I think that that is not a 2013 airplane, I think it is more 2015 or 2016 ... So, I think we have time to assess that plane
finding: In January 2008 Boeing judged only the A350-1000 a real 777 threat and saw it as years away, so it chose to wait (a stance repeated in April and July 2008).
trigger: Airbus A350 XWB orders (250-300) and A350-1000 targeting 777
response: No 777 response in 2008; assess A350-1000 performance first
lag: 7-8 years before rival entry; no action planned in 2008

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think we need to see what the performance of the A-350 might be. We are not just sure. ... I do not think we want to put too many wheels in motion although we are obviously thinking through some contingencies ... I would not see a major program emerging until after this year.
finding: Boeing made its widebody response depend on the rival's demonstrated performance rather than its design goals, and ruled out a major 777 program in 2008.
trigger: A350 design goals announced
response: Contingency planning only; no major program in 2008

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The 737, we have had a steady drum beat that increases there. As you noted, I think we are about 40% higher in 07. It is another 10% higher coming up. And we have the flexibility to go higher.
finding: Boeing raised 737 output in steady increments (about 40% by 2007, another 10% planned) and kept an option to go higher.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: it is a matter of whether our customers need it and whether the business case is sound and making sure our supply chain can catch up, but I think we would have an option of going over 31 if that was the right thing for the business to do it.
finding: Pressed about Airbus's higher narrowbody rate, Boeing set its own tests for a 737 rate above 31 (customer need, business case, supply-chain readiness) rather than matching the rival.
trigger: Airbus moving to ~40 narrowbodies/month
response: Keep option to exceed 31/month; study in 2008

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: I think it is about right the way we have done it and you are going to see the bulk of the better pricing come through at 09
finding: Better pricing from the 2006-07 order boom would reach Boeing's revenue only in 2009 deliveries, a multi-year lag between pricing and earnings.
lag: ~2-3 years from order to delivery pricing

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: So we anticipate success here. We do not anticipate failure. And so none of our plans include an offer up here. All of our plans include making this a success
finding: Asked what it would do if 747-8 passenger orders fell short, Boeing said it had no exit plan, which shows its reluctance to cancel launched programs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In all of our supplier partners, we have got between 50 and 130 Boeing employees working hand in hand, minute by minute, hour by hour 24/7
finding: Boeing responded to 787 supplier failures by embedding 50-130 of its own staff at each major partner.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have absolutely no plans to drop any suppliers. When we qualified our partners early on, we did it with our eyes wide open and they did it with their eyes wide open. We have each put a lot of investment into it, now I think from time to time, we shift work around.
finding: Boeing kept its 787 risk-sharing partners through the crisis and adjusted by shifting work rather than replacing suppliers.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the form of financial support that we might contemplate in extreme circumstances would be more jointly carrying inventory or material together ... We might do it a little bit differently, but the overall strategy would be the same.
finding: Asked whether a 737 follow-on would repeat the 787 partner model, Boeing said the concept would stay the same, and that it would support weak suppliers by sharing inventory rather than investing in them.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We are very mindful of committing to a ramp that we can execute. We are also very mindful that we have already disappointed some of our customers ... So, that tension, I think will produce a realistic but aggressive ramp.
finding: Boeing set the 787 ramp by balancing credibility (a rate it can execute) against pressure from customers already let down.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the US Air Force awarded the KCX tanker program to Northrop Grumman and Airbus parent EADS. On March 11th, we filed a former protest of that award. This was a decision we took very seriously. Boeing had not protested an award with GAO in over a decade.
finding: Boeing fought the EADS tanker win with a GAO protest, a step it had not taken in more than a decade.
trigger: USAF awarded KC-X tanker to Northrop Grumman/EADS
response: Filed formal GAO protest on March 11, 2008

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the A350-1000 as it comes together, it comes together as Airbus has characterized it will in terms of its performance would put some pressure on our longer range 777 fleet and we would have to answer the question what we would do about it.
finding: Boeing accepted that the A350-1000, if it performed as Airbus claimed, would pressure the long-range 777, and said it would have to decide how to respond.
trigger: A350-1000 performance claims
response: Defer 777 modification decision; plenty of time
lag: about 8 years until A350-1000 entry into service

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We will get through to startup of this innovative some would say leading edge program and when we do, we will be delivering a breakthrough new product, years ahead of its competition
finding: Boeing justified pushing through 787 delays by claiming a multi-year technology lead over competitors.

quote: we are engaging with our customers on the impact of the 787 delays and appropriate mitigation plans. This will take time and could ultimately take various forms including the interim lift capability and revised terms on orders.

quote: used $1.2 billion to repurchase 15.6 million shares contributed to our pension plans and paid a 14% higher dividend to our shareholders. Share repurchase will moderate the remainder of the year
finding: Boeing front-loaded buybacks and raised its dividend 14% in 2008 while cash was $12.1B.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: 2009 deliveries will grow to between 500 and 505 airplanes including approximately 25, 787 Dreamliners.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: the prior schedule shift of about 75 787s out of '08 into the '09 or into -- out into outyears now as we now understand the schedule better.
finding: The April 2008 reschedule moved about 75 787 deliveries out of 2008.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Typically when we got to a point of delivering the first airplane we sell it about a 100, this in raw numbers on our new airplane models. ... the initial block turns out to be and about 400 airplane range. ... Well in the case of the 787 we are going to have probably a 1000
finding: Boeing uses a large initial accounting block, sized to firm orders and market potential, which lets the huge 787 order book absorb development and delay costs without a loss.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: in contrast with coming out of 9/11 we are much less than half of our planes were financed Ex-Im internationally. We now have 80% of them financed Ex-Im internationally, which puts us in a stronger position to absorb any financing requirements
finding: Boeing had deliberately shifted its backlog towards ExIm-eligible international buyers, which reduced how much it would have to finance itself in a downturn.

But we have time to make that call.
finding: In early 2008 Boeing paused rate increases after a series of steps but leaned towards a further 737 rate increase, conditional on the economy.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: on the 67, the death of that program has been predicted for many years and the demand over the last couple of years has been strong even without the tanker situation.
finding: Boeing kept the aging 767 in production while demand held, preferring to milk an old product (interim lift, freighters) over ending the line.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We've been forced to keep an experienced set of engineers on that program that had been planned to go on off to other programs. The 47-8 that increased costs as we scrambled to find the engineering capacity we need
finding: 787 recovery held engineers back from other programs, and the resulting engineering shortage raised 747-8 costs, which shows Boeing's development capacity was constrained by talent.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I'm not happy and Scott Carson is not happy with our inability to get our arms around predicting the development cost. The business case for both airplanes remains good
finding: Boeing admitted it could not reliably estimate development cost but kept both the 787 and 747-8 business cases.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We tend to assume that kind of cancellation rate as we put together our business plans and our financial promises.
finding: Boeing builds a post-9/11-scale cancellation rate (about 6%) into its business plans and guidance.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the ramp-up will be slower after that and full rate production in 2012. We're seeing if that could be pulled in.
finding: The re-baselined 787 plan did not reach full-rate production until 2012, and Boeing was looking for ways to accelerate it.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: No, our strategy will be the same. We believe that global leverage is important both from a cost and risk mitigation standpoint. We might draw some lines at different places, now that we understand our own capabilities
finding: Despite the 787 supply-chain failure, Boeing said it would keep its global outsourcing and risk-sharing strategy, only adjusting where it draws the make/buy lines.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: But given the order rates that we continue to have on 777s, I don’t think the marketplace is all really worried about it yet, but it will be an issue we have to address.
finding: Boeing used strong current 777 orders as its signal that no immediate response to the A350 was needed.
trigger: A350-1000 launch
response: No immediate 777 response while orders stay strong

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are asking the questions independently obviously because there are two different, very different market segments, but yes, you could paint a scenario where some work on the 777 would be done before the majority of the work on the next generation 37 but we don’t know yet either.
finding: In 2008 Boeing treated a 777 upgrade and a 737 replacement as separate decisions and allowed that the 777 work might come first.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Results also included cost absorption on our non-787 production programs due to the changes in the 787 delivery schedule we announced in April.
finding: 787 schedule slips increased overhead on Boeing's other production programs, so the delay hurt company-wide margins.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: In our production and delivery planning, we assume we'll see a certain amount of both based on historical data and our judgment about each of the customers in our backlog and the potential impact of things like today's energy prices. We use these factors to determine our production rate in a disciplined manner
finding: Boeing sets production rates below gross backlog by building expected deferrals and cancellations into its skyline planning.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Our guidance assumes that the initial 787 deliveries in 2009 will have a 0% margin and we will continue to assess this as we approach first delivery next year.
finding: Boeing booked the first 787 deliveries at zero margin and deferred any forward-loss decision until first delivery.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: The 787 has enjoyed great sales success with 896 orders since launch from 58 customers. While new orders have slowed, principally due to the fact that we're quoting positions over 10 years out, we've essentially had no cancellations.
finding: The 787 was sold out more than a decade ahead, so new orders were limited by slot availability, and customers stayed despite the delays.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Commercial airplane's margins are forecasted to be around 11.5% in 2008 and in 2009. This reflects lower R&D costs and strong performance on production and service programs offset by margin dilution from 787 deliveries in 2009.
finding: Boeing expected falling R&D and mature-program profits to offset 787 margin dilution.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We expect total company R&D expense to be between $3.6 and $3.8 billion in 2008. In 2009, R&D will decline over 13% to a range of $3.1 to $3.3 billion.
finding: Boeing planned to cut R&D as 787 and 747-8 development wound down, with no new big program funded in guidance.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the way we're trying to run the company is to have an ongoing productivity program that assumes that when we have stumbles in innovation, which those two represent, that we can largely cover it with a strong productivity program
finding: McNerney's operating model used productivity savings on mature programs to absorb development-program failures so that guidance still held.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We do have a view of the cost in cash that it will take to resolve it. It is in our guidance. The majority of it is resolved within the 87 program, but there are some resolutions that impact current numbers
finding: Boeing handled 787 delay compensation mostly inside 787 program accounting, spreading the cost rather than taking an upfront charge.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: There is, there was only an addition of 200 to the 737 accounting quantity and 25 to the 747.
finding: Boeing extended the 737 and 747 accounting blocks, a sign it expected to keep producing the current 737 for years.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: And the 777—either a refresh or a renovation, based on what we see with our customers and what we see that the A350-1000 is or isn’t, and we’ll have plenty of time to look at that. I think its delivery is in the 15, 16 timeframe.
finding: Boeing tied the timing and scope of any 777 upgrade to how the rival A350-1000 turned out and saw no urgency, since the A350-1000 would not deliver until about 2015-16.
trigger: Airbus A350-1000 targeting 777 market, delivery ~2015-16
response: Wait and see; consider a 777 refresh or renovation later

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: we think we’re going to make our plan in commercial airplanes, but if we don’t, we’ll still make our earnings per share expectations and the guidance we provided you.
finding: Boeing's priority was meeting company EPS guidance, using other segments to offset commercial shortfalls.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have unprecedented customer demand on the 37, and we also have got a well-established supply chain ... we feel comfortable that the unprecedented demand of that airplane can be met with a robust supply chain.
finding: Boeing saw 737 demand as unprecedented and its mature supply chain as able to support higher output, unlike the 787.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: After a second round of federally-mediated talks, a number of issues remained unresolve, with the linchpin being management rights. ... it would be unwise for us to agree to terms in any contract that would restrict our ability to manage our business and respond quickly to market dynamics and global customer needs.
finding: Boeing accepted a costly IAM strike rather than agree to contract terms limiting management rights, putting long-run flexibility ahead of near-term deliveries.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We will not sacrifice our ability to compete for a short-term agreement with our unions
finding: Boeing explicitly ranked long-term cost competitiveness above quickly ending the strike.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: between 5 to 10 deliveries of Boeing wide body commercial aircraft were at risk of slipping out of third quarter because of this galley issue. We have been working with the supplier to help it prioritize and improve its production processes.
finding: A single customer-furnished galley supplier was gating widebody deliveries, and Boeing responded by embedding with the supplier rather than switching sources.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Our backlog grew to a new record of $349 billion, up 7% year-to-date. Commercial airplanes backlog of $276 billion increased 8% year-to-date and remains diverse by region, product type, and customer. Only about 10% of commercial backlog in dollar terms is with US Airlines.
finding: Boeing framed its resilience going into the 2008 downturn around a record, internationally diversified backlog.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: So far in 2008, we’ve only had two cancellations and about 80 deferrals that we’ve accommodated. We’ve had no issues in reassigning the deferred aircraft to other customers
finding: Boeing handled early-crisis deferrals by reslotting aircraft to other customers rather than cutting rates.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are accelerating the drive for productivity gains throughout our business and are focused on maintaining our balance sheet strength, which includes over $7 billion of cash and marketable securities and a conservative debt level. We will be very selective in our future investments
finding: Facing the credit crisis, Boeing's reflex was to protect the balance sheet and become more selective on new investment.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: Over the past few years, we have been preparing ourselves to step back into the financing business and will do so when appropriate.
finding: Boeing planned to use its captive finance arm (BCC) as a countercyclical backstop for customer financing when markets closed.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Those issues reduced third quarter deliveries by about 35 airplanes and BCA revenue by an estimated $2.1 billion. Earnings per share declined 33% to $0.96 per share with operating margins of 7.5%.
finding: The strike plus galley shortage cost about 35 deliveries and $2.1B of commercial revenue in one quarter.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: resulted in higher 747-8 program costs during the quarter. In light of this, BCA has increased its focus on improving productivity and accelerating cost reductions.
finding: The 747-8 derivative was already showing schedule and cost pressure in 2008, and Boeing's response was cost reduction rather than restructuring the program.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: BCA R&D was $70 million higher than the same period last year due to the absence of R&D supplier cost sharing payments in the third quarter of 2008.
finding: Boeing's reported R&D was offset by supplier cost-sharing payments, which shows that risk-sharing partners co-funded development.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: it is very likely that BCC will do some new financing in 2009. We will be disciplined in this process and work with BCA to determine the deals that make the most sense. We will also be mindful of preserving our current credit ratings.
finding: Boeing would provide customer financing to protect deliveries, but capped by concern for its credit ratings.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: As of mid-October, our pension assets were down by about 20% year-to-date. ... we expect to have a reduction in our equity which could be several billion dollars.
finding: The 2008 market crash created a multi-billion pension hit to equity, adding to balance-sheet pressure.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: The strike and galley shortage reduced operating cash flow in the quarter by an estimated $1.3 billion. Balance cash deployment remains a focus area for us. We continued to invest in growth programs, used approximately $500 million to repurchase 7.9 million shares, and paid $295 million in dividends.
finding: Boeing kept buying back stock and paying dividends even while the strike drove operating cash flow negative.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: if we excluded the strike impact and if we excluded the slide out, the program margins would have been 11%, about 11.1% in the operating. So and the pre-R&D margin would have been in the range we’ve always talked about around 30%.
finding: Underlying commercial program margins were about 11% operating and about 30% before R&D, which shows how profitable mature programs were.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have steadily increased production rates in a measured way over the last few years, as you know. We have tried hard to meet demand without getting beyond our headlights
finding: Boeing's rate policy was to increase output in measured steps and deliberately stay below peak demand, a stance it said now protected it in the downturn.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The supply chain has largely healed up in terms of having caught up with the whole schedule and was largely caught up before the impact of the strike ... But the gating item has become now the assembly of the early airplanes in our factory
finding: By late 2008 the 787 bottleneck had moved from suppliers to Boeing's own final assembly of the early airplanes.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: about roughly 40% of it is overseas banks, Europe regional banks in other parts of the world, lessors are about 20% of it, capital markets as you’d imagined are not in business right now, XM is another 20%
finding: Boeing's delivery financing was spread across banks, lessors and ExIm, with BCC as a cushion, so it was not dependent on capital markets.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: we were at peak rates before, so to be able to make up that in any short timeframe is nearly impossible.
finding: Running at peak rates left Boeing no surge capacity to recover deliveries lost to the strike.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: on September 10, the Department of Defense withdrew the tanker competition. Given the timing considerations for the current administration and the substandard findings of the GAO, we feel this was a prudent action ... we intend to compete aggressively for this important program.
finding: After the tanker competition was withdrawn following GAO findings, Boeing committed to re-competing aggressively rather than stepping back.

response: Boeing said it would compete aggressively in the new RFP

quote: many of the suppliers have trimmed their production schedule, trimmed their manning levels, and are absorbing a lot of it and why are they doing that, they are doing that because they are participating on winning programs. ... part of our selection criteria for suppliers is their financial strength and wherewithal.
finding: Boeing expected suppliers to absorb strike and reschedule costs themselves and screened suppliers for financial strength, relying on their stake in winning programs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: On the BCA side, I think the 87, we’re trying to learn from that. I think, in retrospect, we bit off more than we could chew. New composites, new design tools, new production process, global responsibility for design as well as production.
finding: The CEO admitted the 787 took on too many new things at once (materials, tools, process, outsourced design), which argues for less concurrent risk on future programs.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: on the defense side, okay, you will not see big fixed price development programs, okay? So that’s one thing that if you add up the challenges we’ve had over the last three or four years, that would explain more than half of them
finding: Boeing swore off big fixed-price development contracts, which it blamed for more than half its recent program problems.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we did not have the kind of controls that we now know we have to have both management and IT to manage globally remote activity and it’s - we are fixing it.
finding: The 787 delays showed Boeing lacked the management and IT controls to run a globally outsourced design and production chain.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: On the -8, we’re not particularly proud of how that is sorting out but we’ll get that program done. And it’s one that - it’s suffered from a few mis-assumptions that we’ve caught up on now
finding: Boeing committed to finishing the troubled 747-8 derivative rather than cancelling it.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: of money that can be saved by replacing a big fleet of 25-year-old airplanes with new technology whether they’re 737s or 777s or 87s with the gas price over $100, the payback is incredibly quick.
finding: Boeing tied new-aircraft demand to high fuel prices: at oil above $100 fleet replacement pays back quickly.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We have settled some and we did better than what we anticipated in those settlements, and so not to say that we have a trend yet.
finding: Boeing's first 787 delay compensation settlements came in below what it had reserved.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: No, that’s why we’re saying that there is none.
finding: Asked whether further 787 delays pushed it towards a forward loss on its zero-program-margin assumption, Boeing denied any forward loss.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we had informally slotted those positions for American, so this does not represent incremental short-term demand rather anticipated short-term demand.
finding: Boeing said the big American Airlines 787 order would not trigger a 787 rate increase because its slots were already planned.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We have provided some liquidity to them. And then those that are in trouble, obviously, different discussions
finding: Boeing gave selective liquidity support to suppliers who performed to the original 787 schedule, and treated struggling suppliers case by case.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: in 2003, the portfolio in BCC was $12 billion; today, it’s down to under $6 billion, so we have capacity. I’m not saying to you that I’m willing to take it back up to $12 billion
finding: Boeing had halved its captive-finance portfolio since 2003 to create countercyclical capacity, but would not commit to rebuilding it fully.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think that issue gets front and center during a time like this when you’re making an investment decision. It probably wasn’t a huge factor.
finding: Labor-disruption risk had not been a major factor in siting the 787, but after the strike Boeing said it now weighs heavily in investment decisions.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the combined orders are somewhere in the neighborhood of about 100 and 110 or so which is, I would say, about average in terms of this stage in a program development. So we - while we’re frustrated by the incremental cost we’re seeing, that doesn’t change our mind about getting this done
finding: Boeing kept building the 747-8 despite rising costs and only about 100-110 orders, and set no minimum order count for continuing.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The work statement on this airplane has expanded since the start of the program to meet performance commitments to our customers, and to recover from our original underestimation of the scope of engineering work that needed to be done on this airplane.
finding: Boeing had underestimated the engineering scope of the 747-8 derivative, which expanded to meet customer performance commitments.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: The 747 reach-forward loss was $685 million. Late maturity of the 747-8 design drove substantial changes for our supply partners.
finding: The late-maturing 747-8 design caused a $685 million reach-forward loss in 4Q 2008, the first of several 747-8 charges.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Approximately 15% is related to later than planned transition of component manufacturing to lower cost suppliers due to their production readiness.
finding: Part of the 747-8 loss came from low-cost suppliers not being ready for production when Boeing moved work to them.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: our plans call for reaching a production rate of ten airplanes per month in 2012, and we will evaluate possibilities to increase and/or accelerate that rate.
finding: In January 2009 Boeing targeted 10 787s/month in 2012 and considered going higher; the target later slid to end-2013.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We both believe it's time to end the era where development programs were stood up to operate as islands of their own.
finding: After the 787 and 747-8 failures Boeing ended the model of autonomous development programs and recentralized functional discipline.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We are targeting these reductions to exceed 6% of our current workforce, or approximately 10,000 positions to support our productivity efforts and infrastructure reduction.
finding: At the start of the crisis Boeing announced about 10,000 job cuts (over 6% of its workforce).

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Operating cash flow for the year was a use of $400 million, reflecting the strike impact of about 2.5 billion and planned inventory buildup on the 787.
finding: The 2008 strike (about $2.5 billion cash impact) plus 787 inventory build drove negative 2008 operating cash flow.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: During the year, we also paid down about $700 million of debt at Boeing Capital, used about $900 million for eight targeted acquisitions and used $2.9 billion to buy back 42 million shares.
finding: In 2008, before the crisis hit, Boeing returned $2.9 billion through buybacks alongside small acquisitions and debt paydown.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Share repurchase will decrease significantly in 2009 to approximately 200 million, which will offset dilution from our compensation plans.
finding: Boeing cut planned 2009 buybacks to about $200 million, just enough to offset compensation-plan dilution.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: Our baseline assumption is that in-production commercial airplane programs remain at stable delivery levels over the next several years. However, our financial guidance does consider risk around operational performance and market uncertainties, including the risk of potentially having to take modest production cuts at BCA.
finding: Entering 2009 Boeing's baseline was to hold rates steady, while embedding a reserve for modest production cuts.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The majority of our production units are 737s. The overbookings there remain with pretty healthy margin of overbookings. If you include some options on top of that, you get up to somewhere in the 15% range.
finding: 737 overbooking plus options ran at about 15% above production entering 2009, the buffer behind holding the rate.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: If we didn't believe that the revenues would outweigh the costs, you are right, we wouldn't go forward with it. I suppose if the airplane didn't have the margin of competitiveness that we see on both the freighter and the passenger side right now, we would stop it.
finding: Boeing's stated cancellation test: continue a program only while expected revenues outweigh remaining costs and it has a competitive edge.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we have long-term order books with financing arranged typically 12 to 18 months in advance. We have significant over-ordering. ... we have visibility on the next ten to 12 months and we feel comfortable with it.
finding: Boeing kept production steady in early 2009 because of long order books, pre-arranged financing and over-ordering, which gave 10-12 months of visibility.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We are assuming in our guidance that BCC will need to do about $1 billion of new financing in 2009.
finding: Boeing budgeted about $1 billion of new customer financing through Boeing Capital for 2009.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are overbooked significantly. Yes, there will be some airlines and some carriers who will want to defer or who will cancel. When you do that math that could end up with a 2% or 3% decline. But the over-ordering we think in most cases will absorb that
finding: Boeing relied on significant overbooking to absorb an expected 2-3% decline from deferrals and cancellations without cutting rates.
trigger: IATA forecast of a 3% traffic decline in 2009
response: Held production rates, absorbing deferrals through overbooking

quote: We focus on producing the airplanes the market demands and we price our products to provide a fair return for our shareholders while continuing to find new ways to improve efficiency and quality.
finding: Boeing's stated product-and-pricing rule is demand-led production priced for a fair shareholder return, not share-at-any-price; the wording recurs in FY2011, FY2015 and FY2016 (pp. 1209, 652, 989).

quote: Our strategy is to leverage our core businesses to capture key next-generation programs while expanding our presence in adjacent and international markets, underscored by an intense focus on growth and productivity.
finding: In 2008 Boeing framed its company-wide strategy as using its core businesses to capture next-generation programs, with growth and productivity as the stated emphasis.

quote: We delivered 104 fewer than expected airplanes due to the IAM strike during 2008. This reduced revenue by approximately $6.4 billion for the twelve months ended December 31, 2008.
finding: The 2008 machinists' strike cost Boeing 104 deliveries and about $6.4B of revenue, showing how exposed its output is to labour disruption.

quote: These airlines have increased the downward pressure on airfares. This results in continued cost pressures for all airlines and price pressure on our products. Major productivity gains are essential to ensure a favorable market position at acceptable profit margins.
finding: Boeing treats low-cost-carrier-driven price pressure as structural and sees productivity gains as the way to keep acceptable margins; the same sentence recurs in FY2011, FY2015 and FY2016 (pp. 1213, 659, 996).

quote: we project a $3.2 trillion market for 29,400 new airplanes over the next 20 years.
finding: Even in the 2008 downturn, Boeing's 20-year demand outlook stayed growth-oriented at 29,400 new airplanes worth $3.2 trillion.

quote: We are focused on improving our processes and continuing cost-reduction efforts. We continue to leverage our extensive customer support services network ... These efforts enhance our ability to pursue pricing strategies that enable us to price competitively.
finding: Boeing answers competitor pricing pressure with cost reduction and its support network, so that it can price competitively; the same answer recurs in FY2011, FY2015 and FY2016 (pp. 1214, 659, 997).
trigger: Aggressive international competitors (Airbus) and intense pricing pressure
response: Process improvement, cost reduction and the support-services network, which enable competitive pricing

quote: As a result of worldwide demand for new aircraft, our aircraft orders have exceeded deliveries during 2008, 2007 and 2006. There may be production rate changes in order to meet the delivery schedules for existing and new airplane programs. This may lead to adding extra production lines, implementing infrastructure changes, seeking additional qualified and skilled employees
finding: Boeing ties rate increases to orders running ahead of deliveries, and expects them to bring extra lines, new infrastructure and hiring.

quote: Commercial aircraft production costs include a significant amount of infrastructure costs, a portion of which do not vary with production rates. As the amount of time needed to produce the accounting quantity decreases, the average cost of the accounting quantity also decreases ... thus increasing the gross margin
finding: Under program accounting, faster production spreads fixed infrastructure cost and raises gross margin, which gives Boeing a built-in incentive to push rates up.

quote: Commercial jet aircraft are normally sold on a firm fixed-price basis with an indexed price escalation clause. While firm fixed-price contracts allow us to benefit from cost savings, they also expose us to the risk of cost overruns.
finding: Because commercial jets are sold at firm fixed prices with escalation, Boeing keeps the gains from cost savings and bears the losses from overruns.

quote: Earnings from operations decreased by $2,398 million in 2008 when compared with 2007, a decrease in operating margins of 6.5 percentage points to 4.2%.
finding: Commercial Airplanes' operating margin fell from 10.7% to 4.2% in 2008 because of the strike, the 787 and 747-8 delays and the 747 charge.

quote: Deliveries of the first 747-8 Freighter moved from the fourth quarter of 2009 into the third quarter of 2010. Delivery of the 747-8 Intercontinental moved from the fourth quarter of 2010 into the second quarter of 2011. The schedule change was caused by design changes, limited availability of engineering resources and the recent IAM strike.
finding: The 747-8 derivative slipped about three quarters because of design changes, limited engineering resources and the strike.

quote: In the third quarter of 2008, we increased our cost estimates to incorporate the anticipated schedule delay and design changes and reduced margins on the 747 program to zero. We experienced further cost growth in the fourth quarter and recorded a charge of $685 million to recognize a reach-forward loss.
finding: Boeing cut 747 margins to zero and then took a $685M reach-forward loss inside a single half-year as the 747-8 derivative's costs grew.

quote: The charge is primarily related to higher than anticipated costs due to late changes to wing design which drove new load requirements into the fuselage and created other statement of work changes for our suppliers. Design and load changes also reduced commonality with 747-400 and resulted in increased costs for components and systems.
finding: The 747-8 loss came from late wing redesign that eroded commonality with the 747-400, showing that a 'derivative' can lose the cost advantage of reuse.

quote: First flight of the 787-8 airplane has moved from the second quarter of 2008 into the second quarter of 2009. Delivery of the first 787 moved from early 2009 into the first quarter of 2010. ... The revised schedule reflects the cumulative impacts of disruption caused by the recent IAM strike, the requirement to replace certain fasteners
finding: During 2008 the 787 slipped a full year, to first flight in Q2 2009 and first delivery in Q1 2010, because of the strike and fastener replacement on top of the earlier problems.

quote: We continue to address challenges associated with assembly of the first few airplanes, including management of our extended global supply chain, completion and integration of traveled work, weight and systems integration.
finding: Boeing names its extended global supply chain and 'traveled work' (unfinished work arriving from suppliers) as core 787 execution problems.
